value_chain_position: Power-generation and grid-equipment OEM (gas/steam/wind turbines plus Grid Solutions HVDC/transformers/switchgear); also co-developing the BWRX-300 SMR with Hitachi — sells the hardware that delivers firm electrons and grid capacity, not a power producer itself
cost_curve_verified: Disagree, and materially. The screening inputs show a trailing-twelve-month EBITDA margin of 20.9% and net-debt-to-EBITDA of −0.85; the company reported an adjusted EBITDA margin of 11.3% in the second quarter of 2026 and guides 12% to 14% for the full year. The gap is a $3,992m pre-tax gain on revaluing the previously held half of Prolec plus a $330m Proficy disposal gain, both booked in the first quarter of 2026 — strip them and clean trailing EBITDA is roughly $4.3–4.4bn (about a 10.5% margin), not $8.66bn. Net cash of $9.16bn as of 30 June 2026 is confirmed against the balance sheet ($13.12bn cash versus $3.96bn total debt).
gm_trajectory: Expanding on rising revenue — the signature of real pricing power. Gross margin went from 20.3% in the second quarter of 2025 to 21.3% in the second quarter of 2026, about 100 basis points wider, while revenue grew 21.9% to $11.10bn from $9.11bn. The company's own adjusted EBITDA margin widened 340 basis points organically to 11.3% in the same quarter, and management said in April 2026 that 2026 gas orders are being priced 10 to 20 points higher per kilowatt than fourth-quarter 2025 orders. This is a supply-constrained producer taking price, not a volume-for-margin trade.
bull_thesis: GE Vernova sells the two scarcest physical things in the electricity build-out — heavy-duty gas turbines and grid equipment — into a three-firm oligopoly where it holds by far the largest installed base. The order book is not a forecast, it is signed: total backlog reached $176 billion at 30 June 2026, up $13 billion in a single quarter and equal to about 3.8 times expected 2026 revenue, with orders of $24.2 billion against $11.1 billion of revenue, a book-to-bill of 2.2 times. Gas turbines under contract have gone 46 gigawatts entering 2025, to 83 leaving it, to 100 at the end of March 2026, to 116 at the end of June, with at least 125 targeted by year-end. Crucially the growth is being sold at rising prices: management guided 2026 orders 10 to 20 points higher per kilowatt than the fourth quarter of 2025, and the accounts confirm it — gross margin widened about 100 basis points year over year on 22% more revenue, and the company added six points of margin to its equipment backlog during 2025, eleven of them in Power. Because these are three-to-five-year cycle products, almost none of that better-priced work has been delivered yet; management has said the higher-margin 2024 and 2025 orders do not begin converting to revenue in force until 2027. The second leg is the service annuity. Services were over 60% of backlog, the power services book alone is $70 billion, and there were 231 gas units on order in April 2026 with more than 100 not yet commissioned — every one of them attaches a decades-long service contract with material-cost escalators built in. Strazik's phrase for it, "a financial floor of demand," is accurate. Third, the grid business is compounding faster than the turbine business: Electrification revenue guidance was raised twice this year to $14.5–15.0 billion at an 18% EBITDA margin, data-centre orders exceeded $5 billion year to date versus roughly $2 billion in all of 2025, and the Prolec transformer acquisition closed in February 2026 at about seven times EBITDA — a genuinely cheap price for the most supply-constrained product in the grid. Fourth, there is unpriced nuclear optionality: the first small modular reactor in construction in North America is pouring its foundation at Ontario Power Generation's Darlington site, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission is expected to issue the Clinch River construction licence as soon as 2026, and the US and Japanese governments announced up to $40 billion for GE Vernova Hitachi units. Fifth, the balance sheet funds all of this without dilution — $13.1 billion of cash against $4.0 billion of debt, roughly $9.2 billion net cash, $3.9 billion returned to shareholders in the first half of 2026 alone. If management delivers the December 2025 plan of $56 billion of revenue at a 20% EBITDA margin by 2028, and the market still pays a grid-and-power multiple for it in 2029, the shares work from here. The conditions that must hold: data-centre and utility capital spending must not digest; the roughly 72 gigawatts sitting in slot reservation agreements rather than firm backlog must convert; the factory ramp to 20 gigawatts of annual output in the third quarter of 2026, then 24 in 2028 and 30 in 2030, must land on schedule; and margins must actually travel from 12–14% this year to 20% by 2028.
bear_thesis: The business is excellent and the price is the problem — and underneath the price there is a cash-flow illusion that very few holders have priced. Start with what the market is paying. At $1,019.74 the enterprise is worth about $264 billion (market value $271.6 billion, less $9.2 billion net cash, plus $1.2 billion minority interest). Against clean trailing EBITDA of roughly $4.4 billion that is about 60 times. Against 2026 guidance — $46 billion of revenue at the 13% midpoint, about $6.0 billion — it is roughly 44 times. Against the company's own 2028 target of $11.2 billion it is 23.5 times, which is exactly what Siemens Energy, the closest competitor with the same gas-plus-grid-plus-wind mix and its own net cash, trades at today on trailing numbers. In other words the shares already discount the full 2028 plan and a good deal of 2029, leaving the buyer paid only for the passage of time. Second, the cash flow is float, not earnings. Free cash flow of $5.1 billion in the second quarter of 2026 beat the roughly $1.2 billion expected, but it arrived with a $6.4 billion working-capital benefit from customer down payments on gas slot reservations. Across the trailing four quarters working capital contributed about $12.5 billion against $12.4 billion of free cash flow — more than all of it. Contract liabilities on the balance sheet stand at $39.9 billion. That is real cash sitting in the $13.1 billion cash balance, but it is customers' money held against equipment not yet built, and it only grows while order intake outruns deliveries. Management's own multi-year target says as much: the December 2025 investor update set cumulative free cash flow of at least $24 billion by 2028, and with 2026 alone now guided at $11.5–12.5 billion, that leaves roughly $6 billion a year for 2027 and 2028 — below 2026. Orders grew 88% organically last quarter; when that decelerates to merely strong, reported cash flow halves even if nothing goes wrong. Third, the order book is softer than the headline. Of 116 gigawatts under contract only about 44 are in formal backlog; the rest are slot reservation agreements, and management has said the classification is "more our classification than the customers'" — a deposit against a slot, forfeited on cancellation, not a delivery contract. Separately, 30 to 35 framework agreements have been under discussion for over a year with, in management's own words as of 22 April 2026, none closed to date. Fourth, commodities are input costs here, and the protection has a seam. Copper, grain-oriented electrical steel and turbine superalloys are bought, not sold; management says prices are locked with suppliers at order, with escalators only in long-term service contracts. That transfers the risk to suppliers across three-to-five-year lead times — and 2025 already carried $300–400 million of tariff and inflation cost. A 300 basis point squeeze on roughly $25 billion of equipment revenue is about $750 million, or 12% of 2026 EBITDA, and on fixed-price backlog there is no recovery mechanism. Fifth, one segment is genuinely impaired: US offshore wind activity was halted by federal action in December 2025, forcing a fresh Vineyard Wind accrual; Dogger Bank completion has slipped to run through 2027; and US onshore orders remain soft. Sixth, capital allocation shows one clear error — $3.6 billion of buybacks in 2025 and $3.9 billion in the first half of 2026, executed while the shares tripled and now roughly 92% above their 200-day average, with three insider sales and no open-market insider purchases. And there is no full-cycle record to appeal to: the company was spun out in April 2024 and has never been tested in a downturn. What confirms the bear: a quarter where gas order intake merely normalises and working capital stops adding, forcing reported free cash flow toward $1.5 billion; a 2027 guidance print near $6 billion of free cash flow at the December 2026 investor update; slot reservations lapsing rather than converting; or a data-centre capital-spending pause among the hyperscalers who account for about 20% of gigawatts under contract.
sop_bull: Favourable sum-of-the-parts (valuing each business line separately), built on 2029 earning power of roughly $13 billion of EBITDA on about $62 billion of revenue — the December 2025 plan hit on schedule and extended one year. Power (gas, nuclear services, steam) $7.2bn of EBITDA at 25 times = $180bn, a premium to Siemens Energy's 23.9 times trailing multiple justified by the larger installed base and the locked service annuity. Electrification (grid equipment plus Prolec) $5.5bn at 28 times = $154bn, between Hubbell at 21.4 times and Eaton at 31.9 times. Wind $0.7bn at 10 times = $7bn. Small modular reactor and nuclear franchise valued as an option at $15bn, roughly what BWX Technologies commands, reflecting Darlington under construction, the Clinch River licence and the US-Japan programme. Net cash built to about $12bn after buybacks; less $1.2bn minority interest. Total about $367bn, or roughly $1,370 a share on 268 million shares, discounted one year at 9% to about $1,255. Rounding to the visible 2029 case gives roughly $1,300 a share.
sop_bear: Adverse sum-of-the-parts, assuming the chain turns against an equipment maker: data-centre and utility capital spending digests, order intake halves, slot reservations lapse rather than convert, tariff and copper/electrical-steel inflation takes 300 basis points off equipment gross margin with no recovery on fixed-price backlog, and the down-payment float reverses as deliveries outrun new deposits. On 2028 revenue of $48bn with margins stalling near today's 13.5% rather than reaching 20% — about $6.5bn of EBITDA — and multiples de-rating to cycle-trough industrial levels: Power $3.9bn at 13 times = $50.7bn; Electrification $2.9bn at 16 times = $46.4bn; Wind carries negative value of about $1.5bn for the remaining offshore loss contracts and warranty exposure; the nuclear option goes to zero as pre-commercial; net cash haircut to $5bn because a large part of the $13.1bn cash balance is customer money against $39.9bn of contract liabilities, and the Prolec debt remains; less $1.2bn minority interest. Total about $99bn, or roughly $370 a share — the full regime-break tail. The nearer, more probable adverse path is a delay rather than a break: the 2028 plan lands two years late at about $7bn of EBITDA and the multiple compresses to 20 times, giving an enterprise value of $140bn plus $9.2bn net cash less $1.2bn minority, about $148bn or roughly $550 a share. The single adverse number carried forward is $540.
sop_breakdown: Base case values the parts on 2028 earning power of about $10.0 billion of EBITDA — the December 2025 plan of $56 billion of revenue at a 20% margin ($11.2 billion) largely delivered but a notch light — at multiples anchored on the true competitor set rather than on the momentum in the shares. Power (gas turbines, the service annuity, nuclear and steam) about $5.6bn of EBITDA at 21 times = $117.6bn, roughly $439 a share. Electrification (transmission, grid systems, grid automation and Prolec transformers) about $4.0bn at 24 times = $96.0bn, roughly $358 a share; the multiple sits between Hubbell at 21.4 times trailing and Eaton at 31.9 times. Wind about $0.5bn at 8 times = $4.0bn, roughly $15 a share, reflecting a segment that only reaches breakeven-plus after the offshore backlog is worked off. Small modular reactor and nuclear franchise carried as a partial option at $6.0bn, roughly $22 a share — real progress at Darlington and Clinch River but no dated commercial revenue. Add net cash of $9.2bn ($34 a share) and subtract $1.2bn of minority interest (about $4 a share). Total roughly $232bn of equity value, or about $865 a share on 268 million diluted shares; rounded to $880 to allow for continued share retirement. Sanity check against the peers: at $880 the enterprise would trade near 21 times 2028 EBITDA, against Siemens Energy at 23.9 times, Hubbell at 21.4 times, Eaton at 31.9 times and BWX Technologies at 33.1 times on trailing figures — reasonable for a business whose 2028 numbers are still a plan rather than a result. At the live price of $1,019.74 the market is instead paying about 23.5 times the 2028 target and roughly 60 times clean trailing EBITDA of $4.4 billion.
risk_reward: Unfavourable at the current price. The shares trade at $1,019.74 against a base-case sum-of-the-parts fair value of about $880, so there is no margin of safety to buy — the base case sits below the market, not above it. The favourable case reaches roughly $1,300 only by capitalising 2029 earning power at premium peer multiples; the single adverse number is $540, with a deeper regime-break tail near $370. The distribution is therefore skewed against the buyer here: modest upside that requires the plan to be beaten and re-rated, against a downside that only requires the order-and-deposit machine to slow. The attractive entry is closer to the 200-day average around $836, which is also where the base-case parts calculation lands.
catalyst_status_note: The load-bearing forward events are non-binding and have been serially extended. On the call of 22 April 2026 management confirmed that 30 to 35 framework agreements for long-term turbine commitments remain under discussion and that, in their own words, they have not closed one to date, having been in those conversations "for a period of time." The nuclear items are similarly unbinding as to date and amount: the Nuclear Regulatory Commission construction licence for Clinch River is expected "as soon as 2026" with no fixed date, and the US-Japan announcement of up to $40 billion for GE Vernova Hitachi small modular reactors, disclosed on the same call, is a government framework rather than a purchase order. The one genuinely dated operating milestone — 20 gigawatts of annualised gas turbine output in the third quarter of 2026 — was reaffirmed at the second-quarter results on 22 July 2026, but it is a production run-rate, not a contracted payout. The second-quarter print itself has already occurred and did not re-rate the shares: they were roughly $1,002 to $1,020 on 23 July 2026 and are $1,019.74 today. Note for the record that in this lane the status is descriptive only and carries no weight in the verdict.
peer_comps_note: Measured against the assigned competitor set on trailing enterprise value to EBITDA (enterprise value divided by earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation), as of 4 August 2026: Siemens Energy 23.9 times, Hubbell 21.4 times, Eaton 31.9 times, BWX Technologies 33.1 times. On revenue: Siemens Energy 3.0 times, Hubbell 5.0 times, BWX Technologies 5.1 times, Eaton 6.4 times. GE Vernova's enterprise value of about $264 billion is roughly 60 times clean trailing EBITDA of $4.4 billion, about 44 times the $6.0 billion implied by 2026 guidance, and 5.7 times 2026 revenue — that is, the buyer pays Siemens Energy's current trailing multiple on GE Vernova's 2028 target, and nearly twice Siemens Energy's revenue multiple today. Siemens Energy is the fair like-for-like: the same gas-turbine, grid and wind combination, also with net cash, also riding the same demand. GE Vernova deserves a premium for the larger installed base and the richer service annuity; it is difficult to argue it deserves a doubling of the revenue multiple.
consensus_delta: The market and this committee do not disagree about the business — we disagree about what the cash flow is and therefore what the shares are worth. Two specific street assumptions are factually wrong. First, the trailing figures being screened on are fiction. Trailing diluted earnings per share of $34.83 and a trailing EBITDA margin near 21% both embed a $3,992 million pre-tax gain on revaluing the previously held half of Prolec plus a $330 million Proficy disposal gain, both booked in the first quarter of 2026. Clean trailing EBITDA is roughly $4.3 to $4.4 billion, a margin near 10.5%, which is in line with the company's own 12% to 14% guidance and less than half the screened number. Any model, index screen or valuation heuristic anchored on the trailing print is anchored on a one-time accounting event. Second, and more consequential, the street is extrapolating a free-cash-flow run-rate that management has never claimed. Full-year 2026 free-cash-flow guidance was nearly doubled on 22 July 2026 from $6.5–7.5 billion to $11.5–12.5 billion, and the second quarter alone delivered $5.1 billion against roughly $1.2 billion expected. But that quarter carried a $6.4 billion working-capital benefit from customer down payments on gas slot reservations, and across the trailing four quarters working capital supplied about $12.5 billion against $12.4 billion of free cash flow — more than all of it. Contract liabilities stand at $39.9 billion. This is genuine cash, but it is prepayment float that grows only while order intake outruns deliveries. The company's own December 2025 multi-year target of at least $24 billion of cumulative free cash flow by 2028 implies roughly $6 billion a year in 2027 and 2028, below 2026. Where we most likely part company with the bulls is on what happens to the multiple when that arithmetic becomes visible. Where we part company with the bears is on the business itself: gross margin expanding about 100 basis points on 22% more revenue, with realised prices up 10 to 20 points per kilowatt, is pricing power in a supply-constrained niche and it is not in doubt. Note also that our base-case fair value of about $880 sits below the lowest fresh street target on file — $949 from Maheep Mandloi on 24 July 2026 — against a consensus of $1,256 and a high of $1,450. We are more bearish than the most bearish published analyst, and the reason is the composition of the cash flow rather than any doubt about the order book.
valley_of_death: There is no cash-burn hump and no maturity wall — with $13.1 billion of cash against $4.0 billion of total debt and roughly $9.2 billion of net cash, solvency is not a question here. The risky window over the next three to nine months is entirely about the rate of change in orders and deposits, and it is unusually well telegraphed. Three specific pressure points. First, the third-quarter 2026 result in late October must show the 20 gigawatt annualised gas turbine output run-rate actually arriving; management has promised that quarter specifically since April 2025, and it now carries the credibility of five reaffirmations. A slip would be the first broken operational promise in the company's short public life. Second, and more likely to hurt, the working-capital contribution is very hard to repeat. Second-quarter orders grew 88% organically; when intake decelerates to merely strong, the down-payment inflow stops growing and reported free cash flow converges toward earnings, which run near half the current pace. A quarter printing $1.5 billion of free cash flow after two quarters near $5 billion would read as a collapse to a shareholder base that has been taught to expect the raise. Third, the December 2026 investor update sets 2027 guidance. If 2027 free cash flow is framed near $6 billion against 2026's $12 billion — which is what the existing multi-year target implies — the market must confront the float mechanic directly, at a moment when the shares are priced on the 2028 plan. Alongside these, watch tariffs and input costs (2025 already carried $300 to $400 million of tariff and inflation cost, and the Section 232 wind and solar tariff outcome was still open in April 2026), the possibility of slot reservations lapsing rather than converting, and any pause in hyperscaler data-centre capital spending, since data centres account for roughly 20% of gigawatts under contract and more than $5 billion of Electrification orders year to date. Finally, note the shares are already flat over three months — $1,019.74 today against a 50-day average of $1,024.82 — and about 15% below the 52-week high of $1,195.94. Momentum has stalled ahead of these tests, not after them.
positioning_washout: There is no mechanical forced-selling dynamic here, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. This is a $272 billion S&P 500 constituent trading roughly $1.1 billion a day, with an investment-grade balance sheet, a dividend that was doubled rather than cut, and no covenant, rating or index-eligibility pressure of any kind. There is no yield-focused shareholder base to expel — the dividend of $0.50 a quarter yields about 0.2%, so no income fund owns this for the coupon. The realistic pressure is discretionary rather than mechanical: the register is dominated by growth, momentum and thematic artificial-intelligence-power funds that bought a stock which has roughly doubled off its 52-week low of $530.16 and sits 92% above its 200-day average of $836.50. That base does not liquidate on a valuation argument, but it does liquidate on a change in the rate of change — a decelerating order print, a cash-flow guidance that does not go up, or a broad data-centre capital-spending scare would produce simultaneous outflows from every power-and-grid thematic fund at once. The company itself has been the marginal buyer, retiring $3.6 billion of stock in 2025 and $3.9 billion in the first half of 2026 with a $10 billion authorisation outstanding; that support is real but it is also the classic industrial error of buying at the top of the cycle, and it will not offset a thematic unwind. Insiders have provided no counterweight — three open-market sales totalling 12,452 shares and no open-market purchases.
forcing_function: The re-rating trigger is a date-certain sequence rather than a single event, and it runs against the buyer at this price. The near date is the third-quarter 2026 result in late October 2026, which must confirm the 20 gigawatt annualised gas output run-rate management has promised for that specific quarter since April 2025, and which will show whether the down-payment inflow that produced $5.1 billion of second-quarter free cash flow repeats or normalises. The decisive date is the December 2026 investor update, the successor to the 9 December 2025 event that set the 2028 targets of $56 billion of revenue, a 20% adjusted EBITDA margin and at least $24 billion of cumulative free cash flow. That is where 2027 guidance gets set, and where the gap between a 2026 free-cash-flow guide of $11.5 to $12.5 billion and a multi-year cumulative target implying roughly $6 billion a year thereafter must either be raised away or acknowledged. A third, softer trigger is the conversion of the 30 to 35 framework agreements: the first one signed would be a genuine step-change in visibility, and management has been unable to close one for more than a year. Nuclear provides an upside trigger without a firm date — the Nuclear Regulatory Commission construction licence for Clinch River is expected as soon as 2026, and progress on the US-Japan programme of up to $40 billion for GE Vernova Hitachi reactors would put a number on an option the base case only partly credits. For a buyer, the level that matters more than any of these is price: the 200-day average near $836 coincides with where the parts calculation lands, and that is the level at which this franchise becomes an investment rather than a subscription to a plan.
moderator_conclusion: GE Vernova is one of the highest-quality industrial franchises available anywhere, and at $1,019.74 it is not an investment we should make today. Take the two judgements separately. On the business, the evidence is close to unambiguous. This is the scarce asset in the electricity build-out — a three-firm heavy-duty gas turbine oligopoly in which GE Vernova has by a wide margin the largest installed base, coupled to a grid-equipment business growing faster still. The order book is signed rather than forecast: backlog of $176 billion at 30 June 2026, up $13 billion in one quarter and equal to about 3.8 times expected annual revenue, with orders of $24.2 billion against $11.1 billion of revenue. Gigawatts of gas under contract have gone from 46 entering 2025 to 116 in June 2026. And the margin evidence confirms it is price, not just volume: gross margin widened about 100 basis points year over year on 22% more revenue, the adjusted EBITDA margin widened 340 basis points organically, six points of margin were added to the equipment backlog during 2025, and 2026 orders are being priced 10 to 20 points higher per kilowatt than three months earlier. Expanding margin on expanding revenue is a moat getting wider, not one being harvested. Management's record over five quarters is strong — every operational promise met or beaten early, bad news volunteered before analysts found it, a disciplined acquisition of Prolec at about seven times EBITDA, and a balance sheet carrying $9.2 billion of net cash. Two things must nevertheless be said plainly. First, the trailing numbers most screens are reading are not real: trailing earnings per share of $34.83 and a 21% trailing EBITDA margin both embed roughly $4.3 billion of one-time gains from revaluing Prolec and selling Proficy. Clean trailing EBITDA is about $4.4 billion. Second, the spectacular cash flow is customer prepayment float, not earnings: working capital supplied more than the whole of trailing free cash flow, contract liabilities stand at $39.9 billion, and the company's own multi-year target implies 2027 and 2028 run at roughly half the 2026 pace. Neither point is a fraud finding — the disclosure is honest and the cash is real — but both are essential to sizing. On valuation, the arithmetic decides it. The enterprise is worth about $264 billion, which is roughly 60 times clean trailing profit, about 44 times what 2026 guidance implies, and 23.5 times the company's own 2028 target — precisely what Siemens Energy, the closest comparable business, trades at today on trailing figures. Valuing the parts on 2028 earning power at multiples drawn from the actual competitor set gives about $880 a share. The favourable case reaches roughly $1,300 only by capitalising 2029 earnings at premium multiples; the adverse case is $540, with a regime-break tail near $370. We are, notably, below the lowest fresh published target on the street. The call is therefore to wait for the wash-out rather than to buy now, and the level is nameable: about $836, the 200-day average, which is also where the parts calculation lands and which would restore roughly the margin of safety this book requires. The events most likely to produce that level are already scheduled — the third-quarter result in late October 2026, when the promised 20 gigawatt output run-rate and the repeatability of the down-payment inflow are both tested, and the December 2026 investor update, when 2027 guidance must reconcile a $12 billion cash-flow year with a multi-year target implying $6 billion years after it. Nothing here is a reason to dislike the company. It is a reason to be patient with the price.
